canonical_examples.problem: Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2,\mathbf{b}_3 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/191549b963b841cb97bbad9b6c65019d913cc148ed466d3c026cc27eccff1d8d.svg) What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2, \mathbf{c}_3 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{c}_1 = -3\mathbf{b}_2,$ $\mathbf{c}_2=-\mathbf{b}_3,$ and $\mathbf{c}_3 = -4\mathbf{b}_1?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/334e52d3fd172cadf353bd6b3d6f3fe66eb0c722320da14ce6fd11b66cdca79a.svg) we can write $\mathbf{x}$ in terms of the vectors $\mathbf c_1, \mathbf c_2,$ and $\mathbf c_3,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-2{b}_{1}-3{b}_{2}+5{b}_{3} \\  & =-3{b}_{2}+5{b}_{3}-2{b}_{1} \\  & =(-3{b}_{2})-5(-{b}_{3})+\frac{1}{2}(-4{b}_{1}) \\  & ={c}_{1}-5{c}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{c}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/9a0eec63eca72981c016e4c504a49d249b6514e5e4f12e77e7d721282b7b24bb.svg)

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases
canonical_examples.problem: Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/e8c67f642148caf84c01b7ee88fe125c4a5ae37ecae313d01d45c277de51d74b.svg) What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{c}_1 = \mathbf{b}_2-\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{c}_2 = 2\mathbf{b}_1 - 3\mathbf{b}_2?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We are given that

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}={b}_{2}-{b}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}=2{b}_{1}-3{b}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $\mathbf{b}$'s in terms of $\mathbf{c}$'s. Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the equations, we get 

$$
2\mathbf{c}_1+\mathbf{c}_2 = -\mathbf{b}_2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{b}_2 = -2\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\mathbf{c}_1 = \left( -2\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2 \right) - \mathbf{b}_1
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{b}_1 = -3\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2.
$$

Since ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/0e283c9948eacf3e231eef3a3feb355c33f20c3dbfd89e97c530331758af34ad.svg) we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ in terms of the vectors $\mathbf c_1$ and $\mathbf c_2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={b}_{1}-3{b}_{2} \\  & =(-3{c}_{1}-{c}_{2})-3(-2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}) \\  & =-3{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}+6{c}_{1}+3{c}_{2} \\  & =3{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/d8d25ca46df4435c67e7c23e61851e2acd4826b0b2d99d9b54de8b6f2c37ee94.svg)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let's consider the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the vector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/2dabd318dc49628f9333642f06492d3303617a0ea1cade93c0470c7a767121f5.svg)

Now, let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be another basis of $\mathbb{R}^2,$ such that

$$
\mathbf{b}_1 = \mathbf{c}_2 \quad \textrm{and} \quad \mathbf{b}_2 = -2\mathbf{c}_1.
$$

How can we find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}?$

Since ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/3e330c07260a16bc76853ca1d275bbd9759f60179dce22500ee6dd38f326ca20.svg) we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal B$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\  & =-{c}_{2}+2{c}_{1} \\  & =-({c}_{2})-(-2{c}_{1}) \\  & =-{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/5d39ae32e2bad5125e6d7cf8ba7b943f2c926e1f1d6525ce019fd9a40c263bce.svg)

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
Let's consider the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the vector

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/2dabd318dc49628f9333642f06492d3303617a0ea1cade93c0470c7a767121f5.svg)

Now, let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be another basis of $\mathbb{R}^2,$ such that

$$
\mathbf{b}_1 = \mathbf{c}_2 \quad \textrm{and} \quad \mathbf{b}_2 = -2\mathbf{c}_1.
$$

How can we find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}?$

Since ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/3e330c07260a16bc76853ca1d275bbd9759f60179dce22500ee6dd38f326ca20.svg) we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal B$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\  & =-{c}_{2}+2{c}_{1} \\  & =-({c}_{2})-(-2{c}_{1}) \\  & =-{b}_{1}-{b}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/5d39ae32e2bad5125e6d7cf8ba7b943f2c926e1f1d6525ce019fd9a40c263bce.svg)

tutorials.name: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases
tutorials.problem:
Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/bec3577dd261660f2545adb66b9c26fbb520ea60aa6b0337094347dbc1937ff4.svg) What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{b}_1 = 2\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2$ and $\mathbf{b}_2 = \mathbf{c}_1+\mathbf{c}_2?$

Since ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/200509c629fdf3d263ff375722f57ed77012a8a91a58a7e7f507fad3765b3782.svg) we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ in terms of the vectors $\mathbf c_1$ and $\mathbf c_2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5{b}_{1}-2{b}_{2} \\  & =5(2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2})-2({c}_{1}+{c}_{2}) \\  & =10{c}_{1}-5{c}_{2}-2{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2} \\  & =8{c}_{1}-7{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/6bc09e66faaef40bba491f31c9342d4d08a8fb6eb3fd4dd1a3e2acdd77421741.svg)

tutorials.title: Writing a Vector in a Different Basis Given a Linear Relationship Between Two Bases
tutorials.content:
Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ be a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/bec3577dd261660f2545adb66b9c26fbb520ea60aa6b0337094347dbc1937ff4.svg) What are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}= \left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\},$ where $\mathbf{b}_1 = 2\mathbf{c}_1-\mathbf{c}_2$ and $\mathbf{b}_2 = \mathbf{c}_1+\mathbf{c}_2?$

Since ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/200509c629fdf3d263ff375722f57ed77012a8a91a58a7e7f507fad3765b3782.svg) we can write the vector $\mathbf{x}$ in terms of the vectors $\mathbf c_1$ and $\mathbf c_2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5{b}_{1}-2{b}_{2} \\  & =5(2{c}_{1}-{c}_{2})-2({c}_{1}+{c}_{2}) \\  & =10{c}_{1}-5{c}_{2}-2{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2} \\  & =8{c}_{1}-7{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14274943/assets/6bc09e66faaef40bba491f31c9342d4d08a8fb6eb3fd4dd1a3e2acdd77421741.svg)
